newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Hun Sen snubs world, stands strong in Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: Hun Sen snubs world, stands strong in Cambodia.

text.p: Cambodian strongman Hun Sen has again snubbed outside efforts to intervene in his country's crisis, forcing the world either to live with his regime or leave it alone.
It's an unattractive choice, but the better course may be accepting Cambodia's new political reality, diplomats and analysts said.
Rejecting Cambodia and relegating Second Prime Minister Hun Sen to diplomatic oblivion appears too risky to its neighbours and too costly to its benefactors.

"What the international community can do is pretty limited, and there aren't many countries that are universally isolated these days. Cambodia's neighbours don't want Cambodia to be another North Korea," one Western diplomat told Reuters.
"The door has already been opened too wide to slam it shut now," the diplomat said.
Hun Sen, who ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh in a coup exactly two weeks ago, seems to recognise that fact, analysts said.

Faced with the choice between caving in to foreign pressure and risking the possibility of plunging the country into isolation, he has picked the latter -- gambling that no one wants to see Cambodia left to its own devices, they said.
It appears to be a winning wager.

While Hun Sen's actions have drawn criticism from the international community, many countries already appear resigned to supporting him tacitly, if not openly, analysts said, taking some comfort in his assurances that he will replace Ranariddh and hold free and fair elections next year.

It's a message Asian and Western nations want to hear after spending $2 billion on Cambodia's groundbreaking democratic elections in 1993 and pouring in at least $1 billion more since then to support the fledgling democracy and improve social welfare.
"We've invested so much here, we have to get something out of it," said the Western diplomat.
"Japan, Australia, France, Vietnam -- the international community is already supporting him," said one Asian diplomat.
"He's taking a hard line because the signal from donor countries is that they want to work with him."

The only countries who have suspended aid are the United States and Germany, analysts noted, and harsh Western rhetoric has been virtually the sole domain of Washington, which is sending special envoy Stephen Solarz to Asia to discuss the Cambodian crisis.
The Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) has also been vocal, but with limited results.
ASEAN delayed Cambodia's scheduled July entry indefinitely in the wake of the coup and met with King Norodom Sihanouk and Ranariddh in an effort to broker a solution in Phnom Penh.
But on Saturday, the regional club's efforts were halted by Hun Sen, who told three visiting ASEAN foreign ministers that he didn't want their help.
"Hun Sen is being very inflexible," one government official said, and analysts agreed he will stick to his position regardless of what the United States or ASEAN says.

"He's not helping the situation, but he'll keep thickening his veneer of democracy and eventually people will have to buy it," the diplomat said. "They won't enter the isolation of the 1980s. That ideology is gone and no one wants to see Cambodia isolated."

Cambodia was shut off from much of the world from 1975 when the Khmer Rouge launched their disastrous Maoist experiment which left more than one million Cambodians dead. The isolation lasted until 1991 when the United Nations brokered a peace pact that led to democratic elections in 1993.
Hun Sen was a key figure in a Vietnam-backed government which ousted the Khmer Rouge in 1978 and ruled until 1993, when he formed an uneasy post-election coalition with Ranariddh.
But now, analysts said, there is no Cold War and the international community has invested too much in Cambodia to leave it alone.
Khieu Sopheak, an Interior Ministry adviser loyal to Hun Sen, agreed.
"This doesn't mean that Cambodia would be isolated like in the 1980s. It's just the principle of our international relations -- we do not put hands into other country's affairs," he said.
